case.description: Design a serviceable retention arrangement for a replaceable flat scraper plate in a dry reciprocating test fixture. The plate and moving carriage already exist; the plate must be removed for inspection without disassembling the carriage.
case.valued_outcome: Retain the plate within 1 mm of its initial position over twenty manual strokes, then permit removal and return within sixty seconds without touching its marked working edge.
hard_constraints: Do not drill, cut, heat or glue the plate or carriage.
Keep the marked 30 mm working edge exposed.
No added part may extend into the marked stroke clearance.
The carriage must remain attached to its rails.
resources: One carriage, one 100 by 60 by 2 mm scraper plate and an identical spare plate.
Four 80 mm steel strips, six M4 bolts with nuts, two small magnets, four cork pads and 0.5 m of wire.
Hand drill for strips only, pliers, screwdriver, ruler and marker.
Eighty minutes of fabrication time and twenty minutes of observation.
observations: An unretained plate moves 6 mm after five strokes.
The carriage has two existing mounting slots outside the stroke clearance.
Awkward observation: the spare plate looks identical but the supplied magnets hold it less strongly; in the supplied pull check it releases at 3 N instead of 7 N.

openings.claim: Challenge the hypothesis that magnetic attraction is necessary for retention. Magnetic success would establish an instance of M→B, not B→M; weaker spare attraction does not establish either implication universally.
openings.delta: Remove magnets as the retaining dependency. Bend and drill supplied strips into a locating pocket bolted through existing carriage slots, with side/face capture, stops contacting only unmarked regions, and a pivoting rear service gate. Cork pads take up play; positive boundaries carry stroke loads. Open the gate and withdraw using the broad face or unmarked rear edge.
openings.prediction: A geometrically feasible pocket could preserve ≤1 mm displacement for twenty strokes on the spare despite its 3 N magnetic release. The nearest rival, magnetic retention against cork without positive capture, instead depends on attraction/friction. Differing observations are displacement and release during identical spare-plate runs; no rival failure is assumed.
openings.probe: Compare two configurations: ordinary magnet/cork retention and the pocket with magnets absent. First verify exposed working edge, clearance, attached rails and undamaged plate/carriage. Use ruler/marker references, three twenty-stroke spare runs per configuration, checking displacement throughout; perform three timed removal/return checks per configuration wearing supplied thick gloves without touching the working edge. Log gate manipulation and seating failures within the twenty-minute observation allowance.
assumptions: Slot dimensions accept M4 fastening; strip width/thickness permits bending and adequate stiffness. These dimensions and stroke loads are unknown.
Available unmarked contact regions permit opposing stops and face capture entirely outside stroke clearance; pocket seating/play stays within 1 mm.
Supplied bolts/nuts suffice for mounting and a glove-operable gate; fabrication fits eighty minutes.

Defeat: no compliant pocket geometry, deformation or displacement above 1 mm, edge contact, or removal/return above sixty seconds. Insufficient comparison time leaves feasibility unestablished; a time cap alone is not an informative test.

artifact.assessment: One proposed counterexample probe removes magnetic dependence; it is not deployed or demonstrated. Unknown geometry and capacity prevent a preservation claim. Both configurations remain subject to every hard constraint.

openings.claim: Use a slot-mounted mechanical cradle with releasable top keepers, subject to a feasible footprint and strip forming capacity.
openings.delta: Replace dependence on magnetic attraction with contact boundaries at nonworking plate edges. Drill only strips; attach two guide/stop strips through existing carriage slots. Use the remaining two strips as pivoting keepers, secured with the remaining bolts. Cork pads cushion contacts. Leave nonworking grasp areas accessible for gloved removal.
openings.prediction: Nearest rival: magnet retention assisted by cork friction. The cradle predicts similar displacement for both plates despite their differing magnetic pull checks; the rival may lose retention on the spare. Either prediction could fail because stroke loads, friction and cradle stiffness are unknown.
openings.probe: First use ruler and plate to establish whether slot locations, contact boundaries and keeper sweep can fit entirely outside marked clearance while exposing the working edge. Check whether strips can be formed with supplied pliers and bolts fit slots. If feasible, fabricate within eighty minutes. Run one twenty-stroke trial with the original plate and two with the spare, marking initial position and measuring displacement after five and twenty strokes. Perform one original and two gloved spare removal/return checks with stopwatch; verify restored position and edge avoidance. These are one configuration and three checks of each kind, within the observation budget if achievable. A magnetic configuration is only a rival prediction, not an additional tested configuration.
assumptions: Slots accept supplied bolts and permit a cradle layout; dimensions are unprovided.
Strip thickness, formability and stiffness permit boundaries and keepers; unavailable capacity defeats this design.
Keeper rotation and gloved grasp fit outside clearance. Failure requires rejecting this arrangement, not modifying the plate or carriage.
Any displacement over 1 mm, service exceeding sixty seconds, working-edge contact or interference defeats the tested configuration; three runs do not establish broader reliability.

artifact.assessment: Positive mechanical capture is a plausible response to material-dependent magnetic retention. Feasibility remains unresolved until geometry and available strip capacity are checked. The proposed operation is a bounded fixture probe, not deployment approval.

openings.claim: A slot-mounted strip pocket with a swinging face gate could retain either plate and permit gloved removal.
openings.delta: Replace magnet-dependent holding with contact boundaries: three strips constrain nonworking sides; the fourth pivots over a nonworking face region. Use bolts in existing slots, cork at contacts, and a releasable wire closure.
openings.prediction: Unlike magnetic holding, geometric restraint should not weaken with the spare plate. Defeat: displacement exceeds 1 mm, gloved removal/return exceeds sixty seconds, or any constraint is breached.
openings.probe: Before fabrication, map slots and clearance with ruler; proceed only if strips, M4 hardware and gate sweep fit. Configuration A: stationary wire closure. Run three twenty-stroke tests and three removal/return checks; final run uses spare and gloves. Mark and measure initial/final position.
assumptions: Slot dimensions, permissible strip footprint, gate stiffness and stroke loads are unknown. Eighty minutes may be insufficient. No forbidden alteration is permitted.

openings.claim: Hypothesized closing loop: mechanism (oblique wire closure) → demand (stroke force transmitted into attempted plate displacement) → response (displacement tensions wire and rotates gate) → mechanism (greater gate compression and friction).
openings.delta: Change the closure carrier from a stationary anchor to a removable wire loop around a nonworking plate corner, routed to pull the gate closed. Nearest rival: ordinary fixed-preload friction plus the same pocket.
openings.prediction: Linked closure should increase measured resistance after equal initial loading; stationary closure should not. Equal increases or absent gate response show no detected return influence. Defeat: tension loosens the gate, requires over 1 mm travel, or compromises removal.
openings.probe: Configuration B shares A geometry. Remove the response→mechanism edge by restoring A stationary closure, preserving geometric retention. Match initial gate pull force and initial 3 N plate demand using the scale; compare gate position/resistance. Give B three runs/checks, final spare/gloves, within the shared cap.
assumptions: Return influence is unsupported. Routing, force matching within scale resolution, sufficient submillimetre response and gloved loop release require demonstration.

artifact.assessment: Two configurations only. Reject either before strokes if its resource or clearance conditions fail; a time cap alone establishes no feasible informative test.

openings.claim: Explore a removable geometric cage: two strip guides capture accessible nonworking plate margins, a third strip stops longitudinal travel, and a fourth forms a removable gate. Attach the strip assembly through the existing carriage slots. This is a fabrication candidate, not demonstrated retention.
openings.delta: Change the retaining dependency from magnetic attraction or contact friction to boundary contact carried by the slotted carriage and steel strips. Drill strips only; bend them with pliers only if their section permits. Keep the marked working edge and stroke clearance unobstructed, leave the carriage on its rails, and make no plate or carriage alterations.
openings.prediction: If capture gaps and elastic deflection together remain below 1 mm, both plates should remain within the displacement limit despite their differing magnet pull checks. The nearest rival is a bolted strip bridge pressing cork pads against the plate: that rival depends on preload and friction. Movement with low preload but intact capture boundaries would defeat the cage prediction; retention only after tightening would favor friction.
openings.probe: First inspect slot access, strip bendability, available margins and clearance with the ruler. Proceed only if a complete capture geometry is achievable. Compare cage and cork bridge as the two configurations, with at most three twenty-stroke runs and three timed removal/return checks each. Reserve the final run for the spare and its removal for thick gloves. Mark and measure position before and after strokes; use screwdriver release at the gate without touching the working edge. Reject a candidate above 1 mm or sixty seconds. Stop if fabrication exceeds eighty minutes or observations exceed twenty minutes; insufficient completed comparisons remain inconclusive.
assumptions: Existing slots accept the supplied bolts and permit strip attachment without obstructing rails or stroke clearance.
Unmarked margins permit capture in every escape direction; strip stiffness, achievable gaps and glove access are unknown.
Three checks cannot establish dependable service performance.

artifact.assessment: The weak spare makes magnetic interchangeability doubtful. Mechanical capture offers a discriminating candidate, but unknown attachment geometry and strip capacity prevent a feasibility claim.
